item.mechanism: Phase separation and surface segregation of Au and Cu are driven by their low surface energies, which minimize total energy, while kinetic effects (atomic diffusion) dominate over thermodynamic entropy stabilization at high temperatures.
item.system: AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy nanoalloys (HENA) with mean composition ≈Au20Co28Cu11Ni20Pt21
item.operating_conditions: Temperatures from 298 K to 973 K; in situ heating; vacuum environment; as-prepared multi-twinned FCC nanostructures
item.supporting_observation: High-contrast areas appear at the surface of merged NPs at 773–873 K, and complete loss of Au and Cu occurs at 973 K due to melting/evaporation of the surface layer.
item.scope_limits: Does not hold for the initial as-prepared state at low temperatures where the solid solution is stable; the mechanism is kinetic-driven rather than thermodynamic equilibrium-driven during short fabrication times.
item.alternatives_considered: Sluggish diffusion kinetics expected in HENA; entropy stabilization of the solid solution phase.
quotes: segregation of Au and Cu at the surface of NPs progressively appears with temperature which clearly indicates that kinetic effects play a key role
Cu and Au are the metals with the lowest surface energies and their segregation at the surface tends to minimize the total energy
the FCC structure observed in the present HENA fabricated by PLD at 873 K is governed by kinetic effects rather than entropy stabilization

item.mechanism: Coalescence of nanoparticles enhances atomic diffusion and segregation, particularly in the neck region between merging particles, leading to more pronounced phase separation than in isolated particles.
item.system: AuCoCuNiPt HENA nanoparticles (specifically those undergoing coalescence)
item.operating_conditions: Temperatures above 673 K; coalescence events observed at 773 K, 873 K, and 973 K; in situ STEM heating
item.supporting_observation: High-contrast areas (Au-Cu segregation) are exclusively observed in coalesced nanostructures, and MD simulations show higher self-diffusivity of Au in the neck region.
item.scope_limits: Does not apply to isolated nanoparticles that have not undergone coalescence; the effect is specific to the restructuring and neck formation during merging.
item.alternatives_considered: Ostwald ripening (deemed negligible as dissolution of small NPs was never observed); diffusion in single isolated particles.
quotes: phase separation is frequently observed during the coalescence of two sup‐5 nm NPs at 773 and 873 K
the stronger segregation of Au and Cu observed both experimentally and theoretically in coalesced HENA is most likely due to the reshaping of the nanostructures that boost atomic diffusion
a higher D self is revealed in the neck region close to the interface between the two NPs

item.mechanism: Atomic diffusion in AuCoCuNiPt HENA is not sluggish; it is surprisingly more active than in monometallic or bimetallic subsystems, facilitating rapid reshaping and coalescence at lower temperatures.
item.system: AuCoCuNiPt HENA compared to CoPt, AuCu, and Au monometallic/bimetallic NPs
item.operating_conditions: Temperatures from 673 K to 973 K; in situ heating on amorphous SiN substrate; PLD-fabricated particles
item.supporting_observation: Reshaping and coalescence occur at 673 K in HENA, whereas they are observed above 873 K in the subsystems; size distribution widens and density decreases rapidly with temperature.
item.scope_limits: The conclusion of non-sluggish diffusion is specific to this composition and size range; the authors note it likely depends on composition, size, and local environment.
item.alternatives_considered: The hypothesis of sluggish atomic diffusion in HENA due to lattice distortions and crystal defects.
quotes: atomic diffusion that is surprisingly more active in these quinary nanoalloys than in monometallic and bimetallic subsystems
reshaping and coalescence processes are observed at only 673 K in the present HENA, whereas they are observed above 873 K in CoPt, AuCu, and Au NPs
the lattice distortions and the many crystal defects in the AuCoCuNiPt nanoalloys do not induce sluggish diffusion kinetics

item.mechanism: Surface energy differences create a driving force for Au and Cu to segregate to the surface, while Co, Ni, and Pt remain stabilized in the bulk due to lower bulk energy states.
item.system: AuCoCuNiPt HENA (4 nm icosahedral NP in simulations)
item.operating_conditions: Temperatures from 400 K to 1500 K; Molecular Dynamics simulations (NVT ensemble); equilibrium configurations
item.supporting_observation: MD simulations show bimodal energy distributions where Co, Ni, and Pt have much lower energy in the bulk, while Au and Cu have smaller energy differences, boosting their surface presence.
item.scope_limits: The alloying effect could not be quantified due to system complexity; the simulation assumes an equiatomic composition which may differ slightly from experimental values.
item.alternatives_considered: Alloying effects (tendency to form homo- or hetero-atomic bounds) which were deemed impossible to quantify easily in this complex system.
quotes: the surface energy, which is directly linked to this difference in energy between surface and bulk atoms, can be considered a major driving force behind segregation
Co, Ni, and Pt atoms in the bulk state have a much lower energy than their counterparts at the surface, thereby favoring strongly their stabilization within the core of the NP
In contrast, surface areas where this segregation is not observed have preserved their faceted aspect

item.mechanism: The melting and evaporation of a surface Au-Cu layer leads to a reduction in nanoparticle size at very high temperatures (973 K).
item.operating_conditions: 973 K; in situ STEM heating; first few minutes after temperature rise
item.supporting_observation: A 22% size reduction of all observed NPs was measured within the first minutes at 973 K, accompanied by a complete loss of Au and Cu detected by EDS.
item.scope_limits: This mechanism is specific to temperatures where Au and Cu melt (973 K); at lower temperatures (up to 873 K), the composition remains stable.
item.alternatives_considered: Ostwald ripening (dissolution of small particles), which was ruled out as a primary cause for size reduction at this stage.
quotes: a complete loss of gold and copper is evidenced by STEM‐EDS, while at lower temperatures the composition of NPs was quite stable
The loss of Au and Cu from the NPs at 973 K is most likely due to the segregation of these two metals at the NP surface followed by the melting and evaporation of the Au‐Cu shell
we measure a size reduction of 22% of all the observed NPs within the first minutes at 973 K

item.mechanism: The structural stability of HENA at high temperatures is compromised by kinetic phase separation, contradicting the expectation that high entropy stabilizes the solid solution.
item.system: AuCoCuNiPt HENA and general high-entropy nanoalloys
item.operating_conditions: High temperatures (up to 973 K); annealing conditions; time scales of minutes to hours
item.supporting_observation: The study distinguishes kinetic and thermodynamic effects, showing that the FCC structure is out-of-equilibrium and tends toward phase separation over time.
item.scope_limits: The conclusion challenges the general assumption of thermal stability for HENA; it suggests that thermodynamic equilibrium requires considering surface energy terms in the Gibbs free energy.
item.alternatives_considered: The theoretical speculation that enhanced thermal stability is due to thermodynamic contributions (high entropy) alone.
quotes: the enhanced thermal stability of nearly equiatomic nanoalloys containing at least 5 metals is nothing more than theoretical speculation
the segregation of Au and Cu at the surface of NPs progressively appears with temperature which clearly indicates that kinetic effects play a key role
this work suggests that if one intends to explain within a thermodynamic framework the atomic structure of small HENA, a surface energy term must be considered

item.mechanism: Lattice distortions and crystal defects in HENA do not induce sluggish diffusion; instead, they may facilitate or have no inhibiting effect on atomic mobility compared to simpler alloys.
item.system: AuCoCuNiPt HENA with multi-twinned, icosahedral, and decahedral structures
item.operating_conditions: Temperatures 673–973 K; in situ heating; comparison with CoPt, AuCu, Au NPs
item.supporting_observation: Direct comparison shows coalescence at 673 K for HENA vs >873 K for subsystems, despite HENA having more defects and lattice distortions.
item.scope_limits: The finding is specific to the measurement method (coalescence/reshaping) and the specific alloy composition; the authors note diffusion properties likely depend on the local environment.
item.alternatives_considered: The expectation that variety of elements and atomic sizes generate lattice distortions that slow down metal segregation and diffusion.
quotes: the variety of elements and atomic sizes generate many lattice distortions and crystalline defects that can create preferential surface reaction sites

this direct comparison with metallic and bimetallic NPs fabricated in the same PLD chamber confirms that the lattice distortions and the many crystal defects in the AuCoCuNiPt nanoalloys do not induce sluggish diffusion kinetics
atomic diffusion in HENA cannot a priori be considered sluggish without experimental or theoretical investigations

item.mechanism: The segregation of Au and Cu is not confined to the first atomic layer but extends into the sub-surface layer, driven by surface energy minimization.
item.system: AuCoCuNiPt HENA (4 nm icosahedral NP in MD simulations)
item.operating_conditions: Temperatures up to 1200 K; MD simulations; equilibrium state
item.supporting_observation: Atomic density profiles of Au show the enriched zone extends over the sub-surface layer; surface concentration of Au and Cu becomes predominant between 1000 and 1200 K.
item.scope_limits: Based on simulation of a specific 4 nm icosahedral NP; the text notes similar trends for sizes 2.1 to 5.2 nm but does not explicitly detail sub-surface depth for all sizes.
item.alternatives_considered: Segregation confined strictly to the outermost surface layer.
quotes: the enriched zone is not confined to the first layer but extends over the sub‐surface layer
Between 1000 and 1200 K, the proportion of copper and gold at the surface becomes predominant and the complete transition from solid to liquid state is observed
As the temperature increases, gold‐ and copper‐enriched zones appear at the surface of the NP
